head:
Programme · Restart

Rebuilding your fitness in 12 weeks

You want to get back into sport, or come back stronger after a quiet spell, and you give yourself twelve weeks. Studies say a lot about what training changes in endurance and strength. They say almost nothing about one specific twelve-week programme. This article keeps the two levels separate: first what is demonstrated, on average, then what we propose on that basis, stating clearly that the proposal itself has not been tested as it stands.

The problem

“Get back into sport” is easy advice to give and hard to follow. As soon as you want to start, the practical questions arrive. How many sessions a week? At what intensity? How long before you see a change? How do you increase without getting injured? The answers you read everywhere look like rules: “80% easy, 20% hard”, “never more than a 10% increase per week”, “three sets of ten”. Some rest on solid evidence. Others were tested and did not hold up. Others have never been tested in someone who is starting again.

Twelve weeks is a practical choice: three blocks of four weeks, long enough for an effect to appear in trials, short enough for you to stick with a plan. No study we read makes it a physiological threshold. So we look at the average gains in controlled trials of comparable length, build a cautious plan from them, and measure it.

The word “average” is the difficulty: it describes a group, not you, and part of what is called difference between people may be nothing more than measurement noise. Many dosing rules also come from athletes who do not have your starting point.

The question

Starting from a low level, by how much can you reasonably improve your endurance and strength in twelve weeks, and how should you organise those weeks (intensity, volume, progression, tests) so that the gain is as likely as possible and the risk of injury as low as possible?

We proceed in six steps, from general to specific: the average effect on endurance, what makes it vary between groups, what varies from one person to another, strength, the organisation of sessions and load, and finally what these studies do not allow us to conclude.

What is at stake

The first issue is health. Observational studies link better cardiorespiratory fitness to a lower risk of death, which is the subject of another article on this site. That link is an association: it does not prove that raising your endurance gains you years. It does, however, justify measuring it and knowing whether it can be improved.

The second is everyday life. Endurance decides whether you climb stairs while talking, strength whether you carry things without hurting yourself. That is reasoning, not a study result, but it is what motivates most people who start again.

The third is a decision issue, and it is the one this article deals with. There are three ways to miss twelve weeks: going too fast (injury interrupts everything), going too gently (no gain, so you give up), or measuring badly (the score of a retest has barely moved, you conclude that it does not work, whereas the test's margin of error was larger than the expected gain). Each mistake costs time and motivation, the two resources that someone starting again lacks most.

Step 1 of 6 · The population

Structured endurance training raises the VO2max of healthy adults, on average

We start with the broadest question. VO2max is the maximum amount of oxygen your body consumes per minute, relative to your body weight: it is the reference measure of endurance. Researchers pooled 28 controlled trials, 723 healthy adults aged 18 to 45 who trained for at least two weeks and whose VO2max had been measured before and after.1

Compared with no training, conventional endurance training raised VO2max by 4.9 mL/kg/min (margin of plus or minus 1.4). Intense interval sessions (HIT, short for high-intensity training) raised it by 5.5 (plus or minus 1.2). Between the two, the advantage of intervals is 1.2 (plus or minus 0.9). The authors describe the first two effects as “large” (“possibly” for endurance, “likely” for intervals), and the advantage of intervals as “possibly small”: probabilistic language, not certainty.1

Once trained, healthy adults gain about 5 mL/kg/min of VO2max, with or without intervals

Mean change in VO2max, with the margin reported by the authors (95% confidence limits, vertical bars). 28 controlled trials, 723 healthy adults aged 18 to 45. Source: Milanović et al., Sports Medicine, 2015.1

What this means

The main lever is training endurance: that accounts for a little under 5 units of gain. The type of session adds little by comparison: the advantage of intervals (1.2) is about a quarter of the training gain (derived calculation: 1.2 divided by 4.9). For a benchmark, 4.9 mL/kg/min is equivalent to about 1.4 MET (4.9 divided by 3.5, derived calculation): enough to go, for example, from about 35 to 40 mL/kg/min (illustrative figure, not study data). These are averages of healthy groups aged 18 to 45, measured in a laboratory: they promise nothing to an individual.

This average hides two questions. For whom is the effect larger or smaller? And is the advantage of intervals found elsewhere? The second step deals with them.

Step 2 of 6 · The groups

The gain depends on the profile, and the advantage of intervals is modest and uncertain

A second meta-analysis, of 53 trials in 1,514 adults aged 19 to 47, separates the profiles: 26 studies in healthy non-athlete adults, 18 in overweight or obese adults, 9 in athletes.2 Against no training, interval training gains healthy adults 5.45 mL/kg/min, overweight or obese adults 3.54, and athletes 1.71. Note: for athletes, the comparison group is their usual training, not no training. That last figure is therefore not comparable with the other two.2

Against moderate continuous training, the advantage of intervals is 2.06 mL/kg/min in healthy adults and 1.07 in overweight or obese adults. For programmes of twelve weeks or more, it is 2.28 (confidence interval 0.11 to 4.45) and 1.83 (0.82 to 2.84).2

Intervals gain more than no training, and a little more than moderate continuous training

Mean difference in VO2max (mL/kg/min). The bars at the bottom show the 95% confidence interval for programmes of 12 weeks or more. 53 trials, 1,514 adults. Source: Wen et al., Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2019.2

What this means

If you start from a low or recreational level, you are in the groups that gain the most against no training (5.45 and 3.54); athletes, close to their ceiling, gain the least. The analysis does not explain the smaller gain in overweight adults, and its authors note that VO2max expressed relative to body weight can inflate some effects through weight loss. The advantage of intervals over continuous training is 1 to 2 mL/kg/min depending on the meta-analyses (1.2; 2.06; 1.83), with an interval that nearly touches zero in healthy adults at twelve weeks: probable, small, not guaranteed.

The authors also report strong heterogeneity between trials (60 to 75%) and probable publication bias: disappointing trials are published less often. These figures are therefore the upper end of the plausible range.2

One finer level remains: in a specific person, what can be expected?

Step 3 of 6 · The individual

From one person to another the gain varies a lot, and part of that gap is measurement noise

The reference study is HERITAGE: sedentary men and women, 20 weeks of a very standardised endurance programme (60 sessions), 720 subjects analysed. The mean VO2max gain is 384 mL of oxygen per minute, with a standard deviation of 202, and the range of responses goes from almost zero to about 1,000 mL.3

With exactly the same programme, individual gains range from almost nothing to more than double the mean

VO2max gain after 20 weeks, 60 sessions, 720 sedentary subjects. The plus or minus one standard deviation band is a derived calculation (384 minus 202 and 384 plus 202). Source: Bouchard and Rankinen, Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise, 2001.3

What this means

Same programme, very different results: the mean gives an order of magnitude, not your result.

Should we conclude that some people do not respond to training? The studies are less clear-cut. An analysis pooling 677 participants from 18 endurance programmes defined a “probable responder” as someone whose VO2peak gains more than a clinically important threshold (3.5 mL/kg/min) plus measurement error, giving a threshold of 5.0 to 5.3 mL/kg/min depending on the programme.4 Result: 31% responders with high-volume intervals, 21% with moderate continuous training, 16% with low-volume intervals.

The mean gain is positive in every group, but few people cross the strict “responder” threshold

Pooled data from 18 interventions, 677 participants (495 men), no control group. Unadjusted gains. Probable responder: gain above 3.5 mL/kg/min plus measurement error (threshold of 5.0 to 5.3). Source: Williams et al., Frontiers in Physiology, 2019.4

What this means

The mean gain is 3.4 or 2.5 mL/kg/min, but the “responder” threshold is 5.0 to 5.3, above the mean. By construction, the majority does not pass it (69% and 79%, derived calculations: 100 minus 31, 100 minus 21), which does not prove that they gained nothing. Limits noted by the authors: no control group, measurement error estimated from a published coefficient of variation (5.6%), and covariates that explain only 17.3% of the variance in response.4

A critical review reminds us that most studies on individual differences have no comparison group: without one, we cannot know how much of the gap is real and how much is random. In the only study with a comparator that it found, differences between individuals were no larger than random variation over the same period.5

What this means

A single retest proves nothing about your “response”, neither one isolated bad figure nor a good one. What informs is the trend over several measurements, compared with the test's margin of error. Does strength follow the same logic?

Step 4 of 6 · Strength

For strength, the number of sets per week and the load matter, not the length of the session

The most direct study on strength is the meta-analysis by Ralston and colleagues: 9 studies, 61 treatment groups, comparing strength gain according to the number of weekly sets.6 Effect size here measures the size of the progression before and after training, in standard deviations: 0.82 for few sets, 0.98 for a medium number, 1.01 for many. The authors conclude a graded relationship: high volume does better than low (difference of 0.18, p = 0.003), and medium volume too (0.15, p = 0.04). For beginner and intermediate men, a low number of sets does not produce comparable gains.6

More sets per week improve strength more, with overlapping intervals

Effect size (before/after training change, in standard deviations) with 95% confidence interval. The medium-volume value comes from a separate analysis in which low volume is 0.83. 9 studies, 61 groups. Source: Ralston et al., Sports Medicine, 2017 (abstract).6

What this means

Getting out of very low volume brings a measurable gain. The step from medium to high is tiny (0.98 versus 1.01) and the intervals overlap: there is no need to aim for maximal volume straight away.

For muscle, a meta-analysis of 15 studies (most lasting 10 to 12 weeks) ranks the gain in mass by weekly sets per muscle: 5.4% under 5 sets, 6.6% for 5 to 9, 9.8% from 10 up. Its authors suggest at least 10 sets, but this advantage disappears when one very influential study is removed, and data beyond 12 sets are scarce.7 For frequency, two sessions a week do better than one (effect of 0.49 versus 0.30, 10 studies).8 A more recent meta-analysis, read only through a commentary, finds a trivial effect (about 0.07) when total volume is equal: frequency matters mainly because it spreads the volume.9

Finally, the network by Currier and colleagues: 178 studies and 5,097 participants (45% women) for strength, 119 studies for muscle. Every prescription tested improves compared with no training. Loads above 80% of maximum load give the most strength (best combination: heavy loads, several sets, three times a week, effect of 1.60, interval of 1.38 to 1.82). For muscle, the prescriptions are equivalent, and untrained people gain a lot without going to failure. The authors do not conclude that all prescriptions are equivalent, and highly trained athletes are excluded.10

What this means

Three things overlap: training strength several times a week works, a medium-to-high number of sets does a little better than a very low number, and heavy load mainly helps maximal strength. No study gives a figure to apply to the letter.

We know what each type of training produces on average. It remains to organise them over time: what share of hard work, what dose, what progression?

Step 5 of 6 · Organisation

Distributing intensity and increasing load without getting injured: what the studies settle and what they leave open

What share of hard sessions?

The “80/20” rule comes from a review of national- or international-level competitive athletes who train 10 to 13 times a week: about 80% of their sessions at low intensity, about 20% at high intensity.11 A 2015 review notes that these data are mostly retrospective, that the “pyramidal” distribution is the most common and the “polarised” one rarer, and concludes that an optimal distribution cannot be identified.12

Trials exist, in athletes. In 48 well-trained endurance athletes, nine weeks of polarised training (68% easy sessions, 26% hard) raised VO2peak by 11.7%, versus 4.8% for an intervals-only programme, with no significant difference in time to exhaustion across the four groups.13 A meta-analysis of three trials finds a moderate advantage of polarised over threshold work for timed performance (effect of -0.66; the negative sign means a shorter time), with low-quality trials.14

What this means

All this evidence comes from well-trained athletes: no study we read tested 80/20 in someone who is starting again. What can be defended is modest: many easy sessions, a minority of hard sessions. The exact share is not demonstrated. Hence our choice to add only one interval session per week, from block 2.

How do you set the dose without equipment?

The CDC describes the “talk test”: at moderate intensity you can talk but not sing; at vigorous intensity you cannot say more than a few words without pausing for breath. On a perceived exertion scale from 0 to 10, moderate is 5 or 6 and vigorous starts at 7 or 8.15 A review indicates that this test identifies intensities close to the ventilatory thresholds.16 But a systematic review (10 studies, small samples, cardiopulmonary patients) finds correlations of 0.37 to 0.83 with the threshold and concludes with caution.17 It is a useful, approximate marker.

On safety, a study of 4,846 supervised coronary patients (175,820 hours of exercise) counts one fatal cardiac arrest per 129,456 hours of moderate exercise and two non-fatal ones per 46,364 hours of intervals, with no heart attack; its authors judge the risk low.18 It says nothing about your situation: with a medical condition, medical advice decides.

How do you increase load?

The “10% rule” has been tested. In a randomised trial of 532 novice runners, a 13-week progressive programme based on it produced 20.8% injured, versus 20.3% for a standard 8-week programme (p = 0.90).19 In a cohort of 874 novices followed for a year (202 injured), the overall differences between three levels of distance increase over two weeks (under 10%, 10 to 30%, over 30%) are not significant. For distance-related injuries, over 30% versus under 10% gives a risk ratio of 1.59 (0.96 to 2.66, p = 0.07). The authors, who call it an exploratory study, suggest staying under a 30% increase per week.20

Neither the 10% rule nor the 30% threshold has been shown to be protective

On the left: randomised trial, 532 novice runners, Buist et al., American Journal of Sports Medicine, 2008. On the right: cohort of 874 novice runners, 202 injured, risk ratio with 95% confidence interval (the bar crosses 1), Nielsen et al., JOSPT, 2014.19,20

What this means

The 10% rule did not reduce injuries in the novices tested, and the 30% threshold remains a lead: the risk could be 59% higher, but the interval runs from 4% lower to 166% higher (derived from 0.96 and 2.66). Avoid sudden jumps without clinging to a percentage. These two studies concern running in novices, not strength.

One author argues that non-contact injuries come rather from an unsuitable programme, with rapid load increases, than from training itself.21 His acute-to-chronic workload ratio is criticised: a study of elite female footballers and pentathletes points out a methodological problem (mathematical coupling) and finds no evidence of an “ideal” zone.22 We do not use this ratio.

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

What these studies do not allow us to conclude

Objection 1: these participants do not look like you

The first meta-analysis covers healthy adults aged 18 to 45.1 The responder analysis brings together 677 people, 495 of them men, aged 18 to 81.4 Ralston's conclusion on low volumes concerns beginner and intermediate men, whereas Currier's network includes 45% women.6,10 After 50, or on returning from an illness, pregnancy or injury, these averages transfer less well.

Objection 2: we do not know what happens when everything is done at the same time

All the results above concern endurance alone or strength alone. None of the sources read here deals with what happens when you do both in the same week, which is called concurrent training. Our programme does so: it is a working hypothesis, not a result.

Objection 3: twelve weeks is not a tested duration

Durations range from 2 to 104 weeks depending on the analyses, and no study we read compares twelve-week programmes in three blocks. The plan assembles elements proven on average: it has not been tested as it stands.

The answer to the problem

The question was twofold: by how much can you improve your endurance and strength in twelve weeks, and how should the work be organised?

By how much? In endurance, controlled trials in healthy adults aged 18 to 45 give on average about 5 mL/kg/min of VO2max against no training (3.5 in overweight adults). That is solid in direction, not as a promise on your figure: the gap between individuals is large and part of it is measurement noise. In strength, every programme tested improves compared with no training, with a graded advantage for number of sets and for heavy load for maximal strength. The figures read are effect sizes, not kilos: we cannot announce a strength gain to you.

How? The evidence converges on a few elements: training regularly, doing endurance with a share of intervals whose advantage is small but probable, doing strength with a medium-to-high volume of sets, increasing load without sudden jumps. It does not converge on the exact share of hard sessions, the percentage of increase, or the combination of the two types of training.

Level of certainty. Solid: endurance training raises VO2max on average, strength training raises strength. Probable: intervals add 1 to 2 mL/kg/min, more sets improve strength more up to a point. Open: the ideal distribution of intensity in someone starting again, a progression threshold, the effect of doing everything in parallel. Untested: the programme below.

What to put in place

Medical advice

This is not medical advice. If you have a known condition (cardiac, respiratory, joint, metabolic), ongoing treatment, chest pain, dizziness or abnormal breathlessness on exertion, ask a doctor for advice before starting.

Here is the programme we propose. It is an assembly consistent with the demonstrated averages, not a protocol tested as a whole. Choices that come from no study we read are flagged “proposal”.

Block 1 · Weeks 1 to 4

Building the habit

  • Endurance: 3 easy sessions, at an intensity where you can talk but not sing (perceived exertion of 5 to 6 out of 10).15 Durations of 25, 30, 35 then 35 minutes per session (proposal), i.e. 75, 90, 105 then 105 minutes per week. The ACSM recommends at least 150 minutes per week of moderate intensity: the plan gets close to it in block 3.23
  • Strength: 2 full-body sessions, about 6 sets per main muscle group per week, moderate loads, technique above all (proposal, within Schoenfeld's 5-to-9-set class).7
  • Measurement: THW endurance and strength tests in week 0.
Block 2 · Weeks 5 to 8

Adding a hard session

  • Endurance: 2 easy sessions of 35 to 40 minutes and 1 interval session (10 minutes warm-up, 4 repetitions of 3 minutes hard at 7 or 8 out of 10, only a few words, with 3 easy minutes between each, then cool-down).15 5 repetitions in weeks 7 and 8. The format is a proposal. Total: about 110 to 120 minutes.
  • Strength: 2 sessions, about 8 sets per muscle group per week, heavier loads on movements you have mastered (proposal; heavy loads give the most strength in Currier).10
  • Measurement: same tests in week 6, rested.
Block 3 · Weeks 9 to 12

Consolidating, without adding everything

  • Endurance: 2 easy sessions of 45 minutes (weeks 9 and 10) then 50 (weeks 11 and 12), and 1 session of 4 to 5 repetitions of 4 minutes hard. Total: about 140 to 150 minutes. With 20 minutes hard out of 150, the hard share is about 13% of the time (derived calculation): a minority of hard work, without it being the 80/20 tested in athletes.
  • Strength: 2 sessions, about 10 sets per muscle group per week (the threshold suggested by Schoenfeld, whose advantage disappears in the sensitivity analysis).7
  • Measurement: same tests in week 12.

Progression rules (proposals). Only one variable changes at a time: duration, sets, load or intensity. Weekly endurance duration does not rise by more than 20% from one week to the next, below the 30% of the cohort study.20 A pain that persists stops the session and is discussed with a healthcare professional. A missed week is made up by resuming at the previous one, without doubling.

Lighter version. If five sessions are too many, keep 2 of endurance (including 1 of intervals from block 2) and 2 of strength. The studies read do not say by how much the gain would be reduced.

What the THW tests let you measure. In weeks 0, 6 and 12, you take the page's endurance and strength tests under the same conditions: same time of day, same warm-up, no hard session in the preceding 48 hours (proposal). Three points give a trend, which a single retest does not. To judge a difference, you need to know the test's noise margin: for the Cooper test, a study of 15 amateur runners finds a typical error of 52.2 metres (1.7%), below which a difference should not be attributed to training.24 The margin of the THW tests is not known; to estimate it, take them twice in week 0, a few days apart (proposal). A week-12 score above the starting one by more than that margin is a signal. The choice of weeks 6 and 12 is editorial: no study we read justifies those dates.

What these figures do not say
  • The mean gains come mainly from healthy adults aged 18 to 45, with a majority of men in several analyses. A publication bias was detected in the analysis on intervals.1,4,6
  • No source we read tests a twelve-week programme in three blocks combining endurance and strength: the plan is a proposal.
  • The load progression rules rest on running studies in novices, without a significant result.19,20 Field tests estimate a capacity with a margin of error.

Frequently asked questions

Do I absolutely have to do intervals?

No. Continuous endurance alone gained about 4.9 mL/kg/min in the trials; intervals add on average 1 to 2, with no guarantee.1,2

My score had not moved by week 6. Should I give up?

Nothing in the studies we read says so. A single score is a noisy point.5,24 Check the sessions you kept up and the test's margin, and go through to week 12.

Can you do strength and endurance in the same week?

The programme proposes it, but no source read here has studied it. It is the main gap in this article.

Is the 10% rule wrong?

It did not reduce injuries in 532 novice runners.19 That does not prove that sudden jumps are harmless: a cohort suggests a higher risk beyond 30%, without demonstrating it.20
